items.title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: by Olek Gorajek, Samuel Redai, Yian Shang Intro Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets. Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values. Initial Problem Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required: extensive business knowledge familiarity with experimentation conventions and complex engineering practices This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform. Enter DataJunction To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case. DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers (Beto Dealmeida), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet, have been building out the remaining features of the platform. Architecture Decisions A critical design constraint for building DJ at Netflix was resource scarcity. We refused to compromise on product quality, choosing instead to limit the feature set. Although DJ was clearly capable of addressing many simultaneous problems across diverse use cases, our lack of adequate resources and official support meant we developed it as a side project for over two years. Our hope was that demonstrating its value would eventually secure management attention. API First, UI and Other Interfaces Later A metrics platform doesn’t need a flashy front-end to deliver value — its core is the semantic layer, which stores a consistent set of dimensions and metrics and serves this information through a rich API service. You can see below how we structured the main components of DataJunction in the Netflix implementation. Our DJ services (in the middle) interact with the underlying data (on the left) and supply our access layer with the business definitions in the form of SQL w/ metadata or directly with data depending on the client request. Consistent Graph First, Other Features Later A complete semantic layer system can seem like an octopus, with its tentacles reaching out into many functional areas and can expand from a basic semantic metadata stored for some datasets to full dashboard functionality. Let’s call out some of them: semantic metadata authoring and management and monitoring metric and dimension query / definition generation metric and dimension data generation (requires a query engine) data visualization and data tracking performance optimization (aka caching or materialization) integration layer with other tools and any / all the above functionality served as: UI, API, client libraries, MCP servers and more. Of course it is extremely hard to provide the best in class functionality across all these layers, so with our small “unofficial” team we decided to focus on the most important piece: solid semantic layer engine (and API) with the ability to parse SQL as the input to the graph and generate SQL as the serving layer. That is the core of the system and everything else can be added later with less effort and w/o the need to rebuild the core. Cube as The Perfect Consumption Protocol Analytical multi-dimensional cubes have been a fundamental concept for decades, with their representation integrated across various data processing and analysis platforms. While definitions and features may vary between tools, they all serve the common purpose of encapsulating, or abstracting, a subset of semantic objects. In DataJunction, we adopted cubes as first-class features for two main reasons: their familiarity to users and their suitability as a serving interface. They efficiently deliver both the semantic definitions (of metrics and dimensions) and fast data access. See an example of data “flow” graph (dotted lines) and dimensional relationships graph (solid lines) below. We simplified the creation of basic cubes, allowing them to easily aggregate arbitrary collections of shared metrics and dimensions. Furthermore, accessing, managing, and visualizing these cubes is straightforward for any client integrating with DJ. Custom integrations, such as for Netflix’s internal fast Druid data analysis tool (Data Explorer → see below), became trivial to build, and we also made it easy to materialize these cubes directly in our Druid clusters. One of DJ’s most powerful client integrations is the ability to link any DJ-originating metric definition back to the DJ ecosystem. This creates a valuable feedback loop: troubleshooting and introspecting business dashboards becomes simple if they display DJ-defined metrics that include links back to the definition source. This link then makes inspecting and running ad-hoc analysis, by modifying existing metrics, a trivial process. This integration is not only possible with our inhouse tools, but also with other well known open-source products, like Superset. Experimentation at Netflix Metrics are the backbone of experimentation. They translate data into signals that tell us whether a change is meaningful, safe, and worth scaling. Without trustworthy metrics and dimensions, experiments risk becoming inconclusive or misleading, so a robust metrics layer becomes crucial for data-driven decisions. At Netflix, the original metrics layer integrated into the experimentation platform was overly complicated. Creating new metrics not only required tribal knowledge of experimentation data artifacts, but also familiarity with complex engineering workflows. This unnecessary friction meant that onboarding a single new metric could take weeks, slowing adoption of new metrics and hindering experimentation. This is where DataJunction comes in: it provides a central hub for defining metrics and dimensions that can easily be shared and explored via the semantic graph. It also provides flexible, user-friendly interfaces (including a UI, API, and various clients), making it easy for users to author and manage their metrics and other semantic models. Conclusions With experimentation domain well supported by DataJunction, we would like to take on next steps to unifying of the general analytics at Netflix and to make it easier for Netflix users to both: find and use metric definitions across verticals (defined in DJ) easily access, modify and experiment with new metrics across Netflix data stack That will require building out strong integrations between DJ and other tools, but that has been underway and it is one of the most enjoyable parts of this project, where most of the feature exists and we are simply enabling existing systems to exchange information in a structured and reliable way. With a system like DataJunction our internal LLMs can deliver accountable information about the business metrics as well as explanation of how they are defined and used across Netflix. Related resources: 2023 : DataJunction at Netflix (slide deck) 2025 : DataJunction talk at Data Engineering Open Forum 2025 (video) 2025 : DataJunction: Unifying Experimentation and Analytics (blog) DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: GitHub availability report: September 2026
items.author: Jakub Oleksy
items.content: Our last update covered content through August. We did not publish another in September while other public content addressed the August 17 outage. This edition covers progress over the past two months. The short version of August and September: we reduced shared-database pressure, added overload controls, created headroom for GitHub Actions, expanded failure containment for pull requests, and moved more production workloads to Azure. Significant incidents, a capacity pause, and a missed migration target show that the work is not complete. By October 7, 120 of 160 production services were deployed in Central US, and 13 of 51 primary MySQL databases had moved. Azure also handled 65.4% of read traffic for GitHub’s core application, 48.3% of Git read traffic, and 80.2% of stream-processing traffic. These percentages measure different workloads and should not be added. We paused Central US deployments and traffic increases on September 11 because capacity was uneven across availability zones. Permanent ramps resumed September 18 after temporary relief, but durable capacity work continues, with a goal of unlocking all available capacity by the end of October. We missed our aggressive September 30 goal to deploy every production service there. During a planned database failover, an automated emergency process disconnected Central US database copies and disrupted customers in that region. We disabled that process during planned handoffs while improving recovery. Outside the regional migration, 24 authentication-core tables moved off GitHub’s oldest shared database, removing approximately one million queries per second from its replicas. The database cluster supporting issues and pull requests removed approximately 980 million unnecessary edit-history rows, creating an estimated 1.8 terabytes of recoverable storage. Weekly deadlocks fell approximately 77% from their June peak, and continuous cleanup now prevents the same unbounded growth from returning. Half of sampled pull request traffic can now continue with limited functionality when a shared dependency fails. Production results showed several read operations remained available during a shared-database incident. Database traffic routing can also add capacity automatically during spikes; one group expanded from 14 to 19 instances during a September 23 increase in pull request activity. A production overload control now lets responders protect higher-priority API and web workflows by rejecting lower-priority requests before broader saturation. Operator documentation and training are complete. GitHub Actions also gained operating headroom. Production changes reduced measured Redis operations by approximately 28% and relative CPU by approximately 30%. A separate infrastructure cache reduced Redis bandwidth by 84%, average response time by 66%, median response time for the primary inventory request by 96%, and queued requests by 95%. The August 6 actions outage, August 17 github.com outage, September failover disruption, and controlled capacity pause are reminders that measured improvements matter only when they reduce customer risk under real conditions. The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features. September 13 09:16 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 28 minutes) What happened? Impact summary Duration: approximately 2 hours Customers may have seen requests fail, run slowly, or remain pending when opening or updating issues and pull requests, calling APIs, creating access tokens, starting GitHub Actions workflows, or signing up. ~96% of the customer requests creating issues through the web interface were impacted during the incident window. In addition, 90% of new customer signup and ~4% of actions workflows also experienced intermittent failures. What went wrong and why? A background data-cleanup job increased load on a shared database. The job had a safeguard designed to slow its writes when database replicas fell behind, but the safeguard did not account for incoming load on the primary database server. As a result, the job continued running until the primary reached its connections limit. When the primary ran out of available connections, requests that depended on it could not complete reliably. Two other factors increased the impact and delayed recovery. First, there was no quick timeout on these database calls, so request handlers waited on the stalled database instead of failing fast. Second, a retry loop around token creation kept resending writes that were already failing, which held the database saturated rather than letting it recover. How did we respond? A background data-cleanup job began writing to a shared database. The job’s safeguard monitored replica lag but did not account for load building on the database’s primary server. The primary ran out of available connections, causing requests across dependent services to fail or run slowly. Automated monitoring detected the incident, and we traced the failures to load on the shared database. We reduced internal load and paused the background job. The database recovered, and error rates across the affected services returned to normal. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are implementing additional safeguards to improve database resilience and service availability. These measures will better control background processing based on available database capacity, reduce unnecessary retries during failures, and limit the impact of slow database requests. We are also improving service startup behavior to ensure that temporary database connectivity issues do not unnecessarily affect service recovery. September 28 21:16 UTC (lasting 52 minutes) What happened? Impact summary Duration: approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes This incident impacted Copilot code review across github.com and GHEC data-residency regions. Affected customers saw Copilot remain in a reviewing state without a review appearing, with delays ranging from ~30 minutes to a max of 2 hours. Some reviews on github.com continued to complete normally during the incident, while reviews in data-residency regions did not. Some customers still received delayed error messages for requests made during the incident. What went wrong and why? Copilot code review uses a separate service to run reviews and 2 versions of the results are returned: a limited copy that excludes the review comments and a full copy that includes the completed review. Copilot code review posts reviews only from the full copy. A change to that service began sending the full copy only for some customers. For other customers, only the limited copy was sent. As a result, Copilot code review could not build a review, but reported that the job had completed successfully. The missing review results were not detected due to lack of monitoring. The incident was detected as some of the reviews remained incomplete for more than 30 minutes, triggering an alert to first responders. We mitigated the incident by reverting the change. How did we respond? A change to the service that runs Copilot code reviews began rolling out, and review results stopped appearing on pull requests. The change reached every environment. Reviews began timing out, triggering an alert to the Copilot code review team. We declared an incident. We traced the failures to the change and began reverting it. While the revert completed its required checks, we posted the incident on the GitHub Status page. The revert then reached all the affected regions. We resolved the incident and advised customers to request affected reviews again. How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful? We are strengthening the reliability of Copilot code reviews by adding safeguards throughout the review and delivery process. These improvements will help ensure that completed reviews are delivered successfully, allow failed reviews to recover automatically, and provide earlier notification when issues occur. We are also improving our monitoring and deployment processes so that problems can be identified and addressed more quickly. Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog. The post GitHub availability report: September 2026 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: Authors: Divya Gadde, Ko-Jen Hsiao, Dhaval Patel and Moumita Bhattacharya The motivation for building the Netflix Foundation Model for personalization was laid out in this previous blog post. The Netflix homepage is powered by several specialized models and it requires significant time and resources to maintain and continue innovating on these individual models. Therefore, we decided to centralize member preference learning and have one powerful model learned from comprehensive user interaction histories and content data at a large scale and have this model distribute its learnings to other models. The previous two blog posts(1, 2) focus on the development of the Foundation Model and here we talk about how we integrate the Foundation Model into various applications. We found that there is extensive literature focused on the training and inference of large-scale transformer-based models. However, there remains a significant gap in practical guidance and research on how to effectively and efficiently integrate large models into existing production systems. At Netflix, we experimented with 3 distinct integration approaches — embeddings, subgraph and fine-tuning. The motivation for trying different approaches stems from varying application needs. Specifically, different teams have different latency requirements, tech stack constraints and different appetites for leveraging the full power of a large foundation model. In this blog, we go over the 3 approaches we experimented with and which are now used in production for different use cases. Each integration approach has its own set of motivations, tradeoffs, complexities and learnings. The following sections go into the details of each of these integration approaches. Embeddings from Foundation model Transformer style foundation models naturally lend themselves to generating comprehensive user profile and item representations. Our approach for generating embeddings includes getting the hidden state of the last user event as the profile embedding and weights from the item tower as item embeddings. Netflix has an elaborate set up for refreshing the embeddings every day. First, the Foundation Model is pre-trained from scratch every month. Then, the monthly pre-trained model is fine-tuned everyday based on the latest data. The daily fine-tuning also expands the entity id space to include the newly launching titles. After the daily fine-tuned model is ready, we run batch inference to refresh the profile and item embeddings and publish them to the Embedding Store. An important part of this setup is the embedding stabilization technique (paper). When the pretraining job retrains the model from scratch, the embedding spaces between different runs are completely different due to the random initialization in the model. In addition, the embeddings start to drift when the daily job fine-tunes on the latest data, despite the daily fine-tuning job warm-starting from the previous day’s model. Therefore, it is important to map the embeddings generated everyday into the same embedding space, so that downstream models can consume pre-computed embeddings as features. This embedding approach relies heavily on the Embedding Store, which is a feature store specializing in embeddings built by the platform team at Netflix. The embedding store makes producing and consuming embeddings easy by taking care of versioning and timestamping the embeddings. The Embedding Store also provides various interfaces to access the embeddings offline and online. Embedding Store integration This approach is often the initial and most straightforward way for applications to interact with the Foundation Model. Embeddings can serve as powerful features for other models or for candidate generation, helping to retrieve appealing titles for a user or facilitate title-to-title recommendations. Integrating embeddings as features into existing pipelines is generally well-supported and offers a low barrier to entry. Compared to other integration approaches, using embeddings from the Embedding Store is expected to have a relatively smaller impact on training and inference costs. However, this approach also has some cons. The time gap between embedding computation and downstream model inference can lead to staleness, impacting the freshness of recommendations. This may prevent applications from fully unlocking the benefit of the Foundation Model, especially for use cases requiring real-time adaptability. Overall, the default starting point for leveraging the Foundation Model is through its profile and item embeddings via the Embedding Store, provided that the embeddings’ freshness and stability meet application-specific needs. While embeddings may not leverage the full power of the Foundation Model, they offer a good initial step. Our biggest learning from working on this approach is that embeddings are a low cost and high leverage way of using the Foundation Model. A resilient embedding generation framework and embedding store are essential for updating the embeddings daily and serving them to application models. We found this infrastructure to be so valuable that we stepped up our investment here to build a near-realtime embedding generation framework. This new framework also enables us to update the embeddings based on user actions during the session, making the embeddings and our downstream models more adaptive. Although the near-real time framework cannot be used for very large models, it represents an important direction for addressing embedding staleness and adaptiveness of recommendations. Foundation Model as a Subgraph This approach involves using the Foundation Model as an input to the downstream model i.e. the Foundation Model decoder stack is a subgraph of the application model’s full model graph and hence the name “subgraph integration”. The Foundation Model subgraph processes raw user interaction sequences and outputs representations that are then fed into the downstream model graph. Foundation Model Subgraph integration Applications can fine-tune the Foundation Model subgraph as part of their own training process, potentially leading to better performance than just using static embeddings. In this approach, there is no time gap or staleness between the Foundation Model inference and the application model’s inference, ensuring that the most up-to-date learnings are used. This approach also allows applications to leverage specific layers from the Foundation Model that may not be exposed through the Embedding Store, uncovering more application-specific value. However, the subgraph approach comes with some complexities and trade-offs. To use the Foundation Model as a subgraph, application models need to generate all the features necessary for the subgraph as part of their feature generation process. This can add time, compute and complexity to their feature gen jobs. Merging the Foundation Model as a subgraph also increases the application model size and inference time. To alleviate some of these complexities, the Foundation Model team provides some reusable code and jobs that make the feature generation more compute efficient. To optimize the inference performance, we split the subgraph and ensure it only runs once per profile per request and is shared by all items in the request. Overall, the subgraph approach allows for a deeper integration and enables the applications to harness the full power of the Foundation Model. But it can also make the application’s training code more complex, requiring a trade-off between metric improvement, compute cost, and time. Therefore, we would reserve this approach for high impact use cases where the increase in metric wins compensate for the cost and complexity. Fine-tuning Foundation Model and use directly This approach is similar to fine-tuning LLMs with domain specific data. In the previous blog post, we described how the Foundation Model is trained on a next-token prediction objective, with the tokens being different user interactions. Different interactions are of different importance to various surfaces on the Netflix website. For example, for the ‘Trending now’ row, recent interactions on trending titles might be more important than old interactions. Hence, the Foundation Model can be fine-tuned on more product specific data and then the fine-tuned model can be used to directly power the product. During fine-tuning, application teams can choose to do full parameter fine-tuning or freeze some layers. They can also choose to add a different output head with a different objective. We built a fine-tuning framework to make it easy for application teams to develop their own custom fine-tuned versions of the Foundation Model. Fine-tuned Foundation Model Integration This approach offers the ability to adapt the Foundation Model to application’s specific data and objectives, making it optimized for their use case. A side benefit of this integration approach is that it provides a de facto baseline for new models/applications. Instead of coming up with a new model stack and spending months on feature engineering, new applications can directly utilize fine-tuned foundation models. However, this approach can lead to more models and pipelines to maintain across the organization.The latency and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) of the fine-tuned model must be carefully optimized for the specific application use case. Conclusion We are continuing to innovate on these integration approaches over time. For example, the Machine Learning Platform team is working on near-real time embedding inference capabilities to address the staleness issues with the embedding approach. We are also working on a smaller distilled version of the Foundation Model to reduce the inference latency of the subgraph approach. We also provide a fine-tuning framework to make it easy to fine-tune and leverage the Foundation Model. We also continue to refine and standardize the APIs used in these approaches to make it easy for application teams to use them. Overall, these three integration patterns provide a comprehensive framework for how Netflix applications can interact with and extract value from the Foundation Model. Acknowledgements We thank our stunning colleagues in the Foundation Model team for developing and continuing to innovate on the Foundation Model. We thank our colleagues in the AIMS applications teams for driving the integrations and their valuable feedback and discussions. We also thank our Machine Learning Platform team for building and supporting the infra components to get these approaches up and running in production. Contributors to this work (name in alphabetical order): Davis Shepherd Inbar Naor Jin Wang Jonathan Indig Kevin Zielnicki Luke Wang Mario Garcia-Armas Maryam Esmaeli Michael Tu Nicholas Hortiguera Qiuling Xu Robbie Greuner Roger Menezes Sejoon Oh Trung Nguyen Vito Ostuni Yesu Feng. Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Microsoft and Japan took down a cybercrime network behind over a billion scam messages
items.author: Stevie Bonifield
items.content: We've all gotten a scam text about a nonexistent parking ticket or a fake package delivery, but hopefully you'll start seeing fewer of them. Microsoft says it helped dismantle a marketplace for scammers sending phishing messages like those around the world. Through an investigation with Japan's National Police Agency, it tracked scam activity back to a marketplace called YAM Store and a pair of phishing kits, CoGUI and Iron Man: Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared to … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: Schools across US protest FCC plan that could disconnect kids from Internet
items.author: Jon Brodkin
items.content: Schools and libraries from around the US pleaded with the Federal Communications Commission to drop the idea of ending E-Rate, a $2 billion-a-year program that connects students and library visitors to the Internet. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has criticized school districts for having "experimented with a massive increase in screen time for students," and said E-Rate expanded too far beyond its original purpose of "supporting basic Internet access to schools and libraries for educational purposes." In June, Carr led a 2-1 vote to issue a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) seeking public comment on whether E-Rate should be "limited or sunset to reflect today’s extensive connectivity rates." Carr's proposal could result in E-Rate cutting the discounts that schools and libraries receive for telecom services and equipment, and imposing more restrictions on how E-Rate money can be used. The FCC seeking comment on whether to sunset the program also raises the possibility that Carr might choose to axe E-Rate entirely. Read full article Comments

items.title: Indian VC Firms Are Following Founders to Set Up Shop in Silicon Valley
items.author: M. Sriram
items.content: For 20 years, Anil Advani, a Palo Alto-based lawyer, has worked on the niche project of helping Indian startups incorporate in the United States. Suddenly, though, Advani’s field is a lot less niche: Every week, a dozen Indian founders seek his counsel on moving to the US, more than triple the rate from two years ago. They’re coming for the AI opportunity and all they can learn about the US market. Hot on their heels are Indian VCs. Multiple firms have opened offices in the Bay Area and hired executives just in the last few months. Over the past two years, Indian VCs have made over a hundred investments in US-based companies, a Newcomer calculation shows — a number that would have been unthinkable a few years ago. Read more

items.title: Yandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move
items.author: Marina Elmore
items.content: Following reported strikes on Yandex data centers, claims circulated on the Internet that Russian bot farms and influence operations had been knocked offline. HTTP traffic charts showed steep drops, fueling speculation that the infrastructure damage had stopped these malicious actors. However, aggregate traffic metrics can easily mislead. There are two autonomous system numbers (ASNs) associated with Yandex: AS13238 is used by Yandex’s search engine, while AS200350 runs its cloud services. Using Cloudflare Radar and Bot Management data, we analyzed how these two ASNs were affected — and while both saw drops in traffic, they saw differing impact. Yandex Search (AS13238): The drop in traffic consisted almost entirely of verified search crawlers indexing web pages, images, and site resources. Yandex.Cloud (AS200350): There was a decline in malicious activities like vulnerability scanning and probing, but high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers. While malicious traffic may originate from a particular provider, it does not necessarily tell us who is responsible for the traffic. Understanding why the strikes had little lasting effect on malicious traffic requires analyzing request behavior, rather than just overall traffic patterns. What happened: the effect of the strikes and pre-event baseline Between October 7 and 11, reported Ukrainian drone strikes hit three Yandex facilities in Russia, progressively knocking data centers and network capacity offline. As seen on Cloudflare Radar, this culminated in a near-total collapse of the Yandex network on October 11 when traffic plummeted to 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350). Despite a brief partial recovery, both networks remained disrupted through October 13, settling at 86-90% below normal baselines. (As of October 14 at 18:00 UTC, traffic is at 85% of normal.) A drop in overall HTTP traffic only confirms that the network went down. It does not reveal whether malicious or evasive bots were disrupted. Looking at the pre-event automation baseline, we can see that before the strikes, automated requests accounted for 36.1% of all HTTP traffic observed globally across Cloudflare's network, and 35.8% of traffic from Russian IP addresses. The outage had different effects on automated activity on the two affected ASNs because they served different roles. Yandex Search ASN (AS13238) is used for search index crawling. Cloudflare classified 99.5% of its requests as automated, and 93.6% of its bot requests as Verified. Our analysis showed that traffic from this ASN indexed pages, rendered pages, and rendered images, which is consistent behavior for a search crawler. The Yandex Search ASN supplied about 7% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.05% of the global total. Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350) is a cloud-hosting network and carries a very different mix of automation. Approximately 95.0% of its scored requests were bots, but none of its observed bot requests were verified by Cloudflare. Yandex.Cloud’s bots looked more like software apps: nearly two-thirds of their requests sent data to websites, some identified themselves as JavaScript, Python, or Go programs, and a larger share went to software companies than Yandex’s search bots. The Yandex.Cloud ASN supplied about 2% of Russia-origin bot requests, and just 0.01% of the global total. Impact of the event on overall bot traffic "Bot traffic" refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms. As Yandex’s networks lost capacity, their bot requests fell too. That was expected: nearly all traffic from Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud was automated. While we saw the obvious drop in total traffic, we did not see any evidence linking a global disruption in malicious traffic to the drop in traffic from Yandex. Russia-origin bot requests fell roughly in proportion to the Yandex traffic that went offline, since most requests from those networks were automated. Date UTC+3 Global bot requests (% of all HTTP requests)* Russia-origin bot requests (% of Russia-origin HTTP requests) October 1–6: pre-event baseline 39.4% 50.4% October 7–8: drone strike on Sasovo 39.2% (−0.2%) 48% (-2.4%) October 9: drone strike on Kaluga 39.4% (+0%) 42.5% (-7.9%) October 11: drone strike on Vladimir 39.5% (+0.1%) 42.2% (−8.2%) October 12 39.6% (+0.2%) 43.6% (−6.8%) October 13 39.5% (+0.1%) 42.1% (−8.3%) * Radar reports global traffic by both total HTTP requests, and by HTML requests (an approximation of a page view). The above table reflects total request volume. Impact on Yandex Search ASN (AS13238): less search crawling The decline on Yandex Search ASN was almost entirely search crawling. Sampled requests showed that 78.1% belonged to verified YandexBot, 11.5% to YandexRenderResourcesBot, and 1.9% to YandexImages. Among websites and services, the industry segment that saw the steepest drop was Publishing and Newspapers, where traffic from Yandex networks fell 44%. Approximately 90% of pre-event traffic to news sites from this ASN was YandexBot indexing articles, with 40.5% of Cloudflare customers returning HTTP 403 Forbidden responses because the site owner blocked the crawler. When the Yandex Search ASN went offline, customers simply saw less indexing from Yandex. Impact on Yandex.Cloud ASN (AS200350): legitimate use and migrating malicious traffic Yandex.Cloud displayed a completely different profile. Following the reported strikes, bot traffic from Yandex.Cloud fell about 40%. Several attack-like categories showed especially sharp declines. For example, WordPress plugin probing fell 90% and scanner-identified requests fell 93%. Interestingly (and tellingly), Cloudflare customer blocks on Yandex.Cloud traffic also fell 70% during the event period, suggesting that proportionately less malicious traffic was even hitting the Cloudflare WAF from this ASN. Impact on business verticals Yandex.Cloud’s bot traffic is also interesting when segmented by top request destination industries: Destination industry Bot traffic pre-event Bot traffic during event (Oct 7-13) Change 4xx (client error) HTTP response status share: pre → event Computer software 24.24M 15.18M −37.4% 18.5% → 15.9% Gambling 23.01M 18.80M −18.3% 99.1% → 99.3% Media incl. adult 1.33M 223.1K −83.3% 82.0% → 61.8% Internet and telecom 524.2K 206.5K −60.6% 71.4% → 51.1% Travel / tourism 363.9K 158.1K −56.6% 27.0% → 12.3% Retail / wholesale 316.0K 167.7K −46.9% 71.0% → 55.9% Gaming / computer games 226.3K 63.2K −72.1% 51.4% → 9.2% Publishing / newspapers 90.8K 8.8K −90.3% 90.2% → 61.4% The majority of traffic from the Yandex.Cloud ASN fell into two industry buckets: computer software and gambling. The computer software bucket was predictable for an ASN meant to host third-party applications and software integrations. In fact, we even saw that api.cloudflare.com is a top hostname for Yandex.Cloud request traffic. An overall majority of that traffic succeeded (requests returned 200s) both before and during the event, pointing to legitimate usage. The gambling sector offers the clearest evidence that malicious automation relocated rather than disappeared. Nearly all of Yandex.Cloud’s bot requests were targeted at one gambling customer account, with traffic shifting among its hostnames. Immediately following the October 8 disruption, bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to this account dropped to zero. Simultaneously, identical requests began appearing from other Russian hosting ASNs, including Radist and Selectel. The incoming traffic maintained an identical fingerprint across providers: The same JA4 TLS client fingerprint The same uncommon request paths and HTTP headers The same custom User-Agent strings Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%). The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable. Across most industries, the share of bot requests from Yandex.Cloud returning any HTTP 4xx response fell. This is largely due to a drop off in the attack-like traffic mentioned above. This, in combination with the gambling customer analysis, shows that malicious traffic that was sending requests through Yandex.Cloud simply shifted its “services” to other providers after the service disruption. Finally, when we analyzed social media traffic, we found no unexpected changes in traffic either from Russian-origin IPs (0.6% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.2% increase in total traffic over the event period). We repeated the analysis on bot traffic hitting the “post”, “reply”, and “like” endpoints for a specific social media platform and similarly did not find an unexpected shift before or during the event period from either Russian-origin IPs (5.7% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.1% increase in total traffic over the event period). Based on our assessment, the data does not appear to support the claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though without further analysis with data outside of Cloudflare, we cannot conclusively say there is no connection. What the data told us — and what it didn’t When traffic from Yandex networks collapsed, speculation spread across the Internet that Russian influence operations and malicious botnets had suffered a crippling blow. Cloudflare data tells a different story: across Cloudflare's network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the Internet. Instead, the data demonstrated: Search indexing dropped. The overwhelming majority of the traffic that dropped from Yandex Search ASN consisted of verified YandexBot crawlers fetching news articles and web assets. The main impact was reduced content discovery in Yandex Search. Malicious automation migrated instead of stopping. While vulnerability scanning and plugin probing temporarily dropped on Yandex.Cloud, high-volume operations quickly moved to alternative hosting networks. A network disruption means that specific servers stopped sending requests, but it does not mean an automated threat disappeared. Cloud workloads are portable, so when a data center goes dark or an IP prefix gets blocked, operators can migrate their scripts to another provider in hours. Our analysis here is a reminder that client ASN traffic volume is an unreliable proxy for interpreting automated bot behavior. Defending against automated threats requires inspecting request behavior, such as identifying shared JA4 fingerprints, monitoring anomalous request rates, and applying WAF rules to sensitive endpoints, regardless of which network the request originates from. Physical infrastructure is static, but malicious automation is built to move.

items.title: DHS Inspector General Finds That TSA is Not Properly Safeguarding Passenger Facial Recognition Data
items.author: Sophia Cope
items.content: EFF legal intern Gabrielle Ladun was the principal author of this post. The Department of Homeland Security Office of Inspector General (DHS OIG) has published a summary of findings from its audit of the Transportation Security Administration’s (TSA) facial recognition technology. While the detailed findings are classified, the summary states that the OIG’s audit uncovered a “significant weakness” in the technology’s ability to protect the privacy of passenger data. This has massive privacy implications for the millions of passengers who travel and don’t opt out of the TSA’s biometric surveillance technology verification process. TSA uses facial comparison technology for identity verification of airline passengers. A camera takes a photo of passengers to verify that their provided identification matches their live photo. Although TSA states that it is “committed to protecting traveler privacy,” the audit highlights that this has not been the case. The OIG found that TSA’s Credential Authentication Technology 2’s (CAT-2) vendor “was able to access and extract sensitive passenger information, including driver’s license and passport images, during system troubleshooting and enhancements, without TSA’s knowledge.” The OIG further admonished the agency: TSA lacked clear policies, did not track when this data was extracted, could not verify that extracted information was properly deleted, and did not notify passengers when their biometric and biographic information may have been stored. As a result, although passenger information was generally protected during routine operations, weaknesses in vendor oversight created a risk that sensitive personal information could be retained or exposed. We hope the TSA will fix these issues. The OIG summary states: We issued one finding and three recommendations to strengthen controls, improve oversight, and ensure transparency and the proper handling of passenger data. TSA concurred with all three recommendations. Two recommendations are open and resolved, and one remains open and unresolved. Why EFF Opposes the Government’s Use of Facial Recognition Technology EFF has a long history of opposing governmental use of facial recognition technology. As the OIG’s audit underscores, this technology presents privacy risks associated with unsecured data, unauthorized access, and data breaches. The government’s use of this technology also creates a mass surveillance system and facilitates the creation of warrantless biometric records for unconsenting parties. The biometric data captured by this technology is not without errors. There have been multiple instances of law enforcement agencies using facial recognition technology to misidentify and arrest innocent individuals. Reminder: Opting Out of TSA Photos Is Possible Given that facial recognition technology is prone to mistakes, combined with the OIG’s audit revealing significant privacy weaknesses, it is imperative that travelers remember that opting out is possible. TSA’s own website emphasizes that travelers who wish to decline to have their photo taken for facial comparison can do so without any delay, disruption, or recourse. Considering the data protection weaknesses exposed by the OIG’s audit, EFF will continue to oppose this governmental system of mass surveillance and spread awareness to ensure that no one is forced to relinquish their biometric data without consent.

items.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.author: Brandon Anderson
items.content: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack, and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding, or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is. Their substack — or at least Owl Posting’s1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules.2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint, blog, and open dataset. We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Enjoy! We covered: Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA. The Kaggle competition: about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete. Clever Hans in ChEMBL: models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does. Hermes, trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB. Breaking the pocket: engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites. Lumacaftor-like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins. The agent sandbox: LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100. The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme. The Kosuri paradox: if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets. What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification. 1 The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet. 2 As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

items.title: Things are finally looking up for NASA's first missions to Venus in a generation
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.content: Most planetary scientists will tell you the heyday of Venus exploration was more than a generation ago. That is about to change. Two NASA missions are on track to launch to Venus in the early 2030s. The first, known as the Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging (DAVINCI), is now scheduled for launch in December 2030, a year earlier than previously planned. DAVINCI will send a parachute-assisted descent probe through the atmosphere of Venus, returning the first direct images of the planet's surface since 1982. A second mission, Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy (VERITAS), will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit. The European Space Agency is building another orbiter, Envision, for launch to Venus in 2032. The Venus armada might get started as soon as next year, when Rocket Lab aims to launch a privately funded probe to search for signs of organic material in the planet's clouds. items.title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding. In announcing the new publicly available "Preview" build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that "programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." items.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. The hacks that didn't have to happen Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. Read full article Comments

items.title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.author: Richard MacManus
items.content: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety. Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment, rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim, Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability. “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use.” Joseph Kim at AIE NY; photo by Richard MacManus As for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision. “How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.” Balancing AI Safety and Innovation at a Hedge Fund John Feminella, SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma, is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities. Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make. At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls, which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.” The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.” One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers, which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.” Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases. Anthropic: Give agents context, then define the boundaries of trust Anthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows. Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors, allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills. At AIE this week, Belinda Neal, Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product. “Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.” Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab, who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps: “Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer. How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.” Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval. “We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said. “By building once with a foundational layer that you trust, you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale,” Shahab concluded. Bloomberg: Enforce security outside the model As Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, Andrey Rybka has the responsibility to balance autonomy and scale at the company. In a presentation today at AIE, Rybka talked about a series of real-life events where agents caused havoc — and the defenses that can help prevent it. These include scoped identities and credentials, controls over tool calls, outbound traffic restrictions, audit trails, budgets, and kill switches. In one example, an agent treated instructions embedded in a marketplace review as an instruction to stock a product. Rybka recommended input validation, prompt injection defenses, provenance tracking, and human approval for high-value actions. “We want deterministic controls outside the model,” Rybka said. “Check every call, log it, and keep a kill switch.” Go fast and stop safely Even though frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are building a ‘trust framework’ for financial agents, ultimately it’s up to financial firms to put controls around their agents. Two Sigma’s John Feminella hit the nail on the head: implement controls that enable autonomy to happen, but don’t put up roadblocks. Or as he put it in his conclusion: “Why do cars have brakes? It’s not just so that you can stop, it’s so that you can go fast and stop safely.”

items.title: We’re Asking the Wisconsin Supreme Court to End Warrantless ALPR Searches
items.author: Andrew Crocker
items.content: Today, EFF joined the ACLU of Wisconsin in filing a petition to the Wisconsin Supreme Court, asking it to rule that the state’s constitution requires a warrant for retrospective searches of ALPR databases used by law enforcement in four cities: Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha, and Green Bay. We represent a religious organization, the Wisconsin Council of Churches, as well as an individual pastor in Green Bay. As the petition explains: Right now, Automated License Plate Readers (“ALPRs”) are recording the movements of vast numbers of Wisconsin drivers as they seek medical care, attend 12-step recovery meetings, attend religious services, participate in protests, attend political meetings, and engage in many other private, sensitive activities. Law enforcement entities throughout Wisconsin collect, store, share, and aggregate this ALPR data. Then they search it, retrospectively tracking the movements of individuals and entire communities in ways that would have been prohibitively costly, if not outright impossible, before the advent of ALPR technology. We all deserve to be free of warrantless mass surveillance. We all deserve to live in a country where surveillance vendors cannot help police upend our system of individualized suspicion. Religious organizations and officials like our clients have a heightened interest in protecting their location privacy because of the range of expressive associations their work entails, including facilitating gatherings for religious worship, as well as offering pastoral care, confidential counseling, and community support. Likewise, the people who visit houses of worship have a strong right to privacy against police monitoring of when they pray, seek addiction counseling, or attend a domestic violence survivor meeting. This is our second lawsuit challenging warrantless ALPR searches, following SIREN v. San Jose. Earlier this month, a federal court in Oklahoma became the first to rule that ALPRs are a “type of indiscriminate mass surveillance” and suppress evidence from a warrantless ALPR search. We hope the Wisconsin Supreme Court will agree. Read the Wisconsin Supreme Court petition Read the press release Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay

items.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
items.author: Van Dai Do, Huu Hiep Nguyen, Minh Hoang Nguyen, Manh Nguyen, Hung Le
items.content: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.

items.title: Inverse Reasoning Models for Efficient Post-Training and Verification from Answer-Only Data
items.author: Eric O. Korman
items.content: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.

items.title: Do Vision CIL Methods Transfer to Protein? A Diagnostic Benchmark of Frozen Protein Encoders
items.author: Ziyuan Gao
items.content: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.

items.title: Do Perturbation Predictors Learn Gene Interactions? Diagnosing Extrapolation in Agentic Screening
items.author: Ziyuan Gao
items.content: High-throughput perturbation screens increasingly use machine-learning models to predict the effects of gene combinations that were never measured. A difficult case arises when both genes in a test pair were seen individually during training, but their combination was not. In this setting, standard OOD methods often fail because neither gene appears unfamiliar on its own. We therefore compare each model prediction with a simple additive prediction obtained by summing the two observed single-gene effects. The difference between them, which we call additive disagreement (AD), measures how much extra interaction effect the model introduces for an unseen combination. Across eight prediction methods and three Perturb-seq datasets, specialised neural predictors do not consistently outperform this simple additive baseline. More importantly, predictions with larger deviations from the additive baseline tend to have larger errors. Conventional output-based and embedding-based confidence signals are inconsistent across datasets and models, whereas AD remains informative across all evaluated compositional settings. We further study how this signal can guide decisions in an agentic perturbation-screening workflow. The code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/OOD.

items.title: Following the Flow the Law Requires: Training Voice Agents to Transfer to Unseen Regulated Procedures in Debt Collection
items.author: Petmongkon Pornpichitsuwan, Krittin Pachtrachai, Touchapon Kraisingkorn
items.content: Voice agents built on large language models (LLMs) now handle customer calls, but in regulated applications completing the task is not enough: the agent must follow a conversational flow set by law. In debt collection, it must confirm it is speaking to the debtor before mentioning the debt, identify itself and the creditor, state the amount, and avoid prohibited language. Every creditor turns these rules into its own procedure and revises it. We ask whether a small, self-hosted policy can be trained once and then follow regulated procedures it has never seen. One machine-readable specification per deployment, FlowSpec, generates the policy instruction, gates the tools, supplies the supervision and defines the tests; the agent speaks only approved catalogue sentences. We fine-tune a 9-billion-parameter model on 2,506 conversations from 297 randomized procedures and evaluate a Thai outbound-call agent on four unseen deployment procedures (three debt collection, one non-debt), one from a wholly withheld lineage. Documented checks, fixed by the procedure, rise from 67--71 percents to 93--100 percents, while grounded checks, fixed by the conversation, already pass at 97--100 percents before training; scenario pass rate rises from 15/43 to 40/43. An audit of the shared specification finds 11 defects, 3 of which its own metric did not expose.

items.title: Token Utility for On-Policy Distillation via Local Trust-Region Optimization
items.author: Narayanan Sadagopan, Yilan Chen, Vijay Lingam
items.content: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.

items.title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution
items.author: Fengrui Fan, Huahao Wang, Jingyi Fang, Yutao Hu, Yueming Wu, Deqing Zou
items.content: LLM agent frameworks heavily rely on external skill assets to standardize tool usage, encode operational workflows, and supply executable runtime resources. Despite their widespread adoption, multi-component skill packages frequently suffer from cross-artifact inconsistencies, where documentation, scripts, and configuration files specify conflicting behavioral constraints. Although static auditing techniques can uncover such contractual discrepancies, static defect volume cannot reliably reflect real-world agent performance degradation. This gap leaves practitioners without rigorous evidence to assess the practical risk of flawed agent skills. This paper presents a systematic empirical study to demystify the runtime implications of skill inconsistencies. We conduct large-scale auditing over 575 community and benchmark skills, yielding 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies. We further build a controlled evaluation pipeline with 49 executable agent tasks and three representative LLMs across NoSkill, OriginalSkill, and FixedSkill experimental settings. Through fine-grained behavioral analysis of 441 paired execution trajectories, we quantify the actual performance impacts of resolved defects.

items.title: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
items.author: Robert Tjarko Lange, Luca Grillotti, Yutaro Yamada, Rujikorn Charakorn, David Ha
items.content: Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.

items.title: Beyond Equation Search: Conjecture-Guided Discovery with SCOPE and ClosureBench
items.author: Yuxiao Hu, Qian Li, Ding Wang, Siheng Chen, Linfeng Zhang, Jinyue Yan, Yuntian Chen
items.content: Most symbolic regression methods optimize candidate equations, but improving an equation's fit does not establish whether its underlying scientific conjecture should be retained, revised, or rejected. A conjecture may admit multiple mathematical realizations, and similarly accurate equations may imply different explanations. This motivates a shift from refining individual expressions to developing and testing the conjectures that guide them. We introduce SCOPE, a framework that sustains multiple conjecture-driven research trajectories. Multiple scientist agents independently pursue conjectures through equation modeling, question formulation, and active experimentation, then exchange evidence to revise their conjectures and research directions. Their findings are consolidated into a scientific report linking models, conclusions, and evidence. Existing equation-discovery benchmarks primarily assess recovered expressions, leaving the evidence and scientific conclusions established through the investigation underexamined. We therefore introduce ClosureBench, an interactive benchmark of 60 closure-discovery tasks across five scientific domains. ClosureBench focuses on closure-discovery tasks to give equation discovery a concrete scientific purpose. Each task embeds an unknown algebraic relation in a known PDE system, where agents control experimental conditions in OpenFOAM to acquire new data for equation discovery. Beyond equation accuracy, ClosureBench proposes three metrics to evaluate the discovery process: evidence faithfulness, mechanism insight, and experimental effectiveness.
