items.title: Cloudflare and OpenAI: making AI discovery better for everyone
items.author: Matthew Conroy
items.content: Optimizing your site for AI is of little use if AI can't find it. The answer to someone's question may already be on your website: the installation guide you spent a week writing, or a first-hand account of using a product, with the details that make the difference for whether they buy it. As more people turn to AI for help, you want those systems to find your work, represent it accurately, and send interested people your way. You also want control over how they access your site. Cloudflare and OpenAI launched a research pilot in July 2026 with those interests in mind. We wanted to find out whether signals from Cloudflare’s network could help ChatGPT users discover new content more efficiently. Today, we’re sharing early results. So far, the answer is a resounding yes: the pilot has brought previously unknown pages into OpenAI’s search index, giving ChatGPT more sources to draw on to help people find relevant, timely information. Along the way, we’ve learned more about what makes a page worth discovering and how AI systems use the web. Finding more of the web The web is full of specifics. Someone fixing a washing machine needs the manual for their exact model. Someone applying for a passport needs the current requirements and fees. Someone choosing a local restaurant needs its latest menu and opening hours. Finding the right page can be the difference between a wrong answer and one that actually helps. These pages can be valuable even if few other sites link to them. In the previous version of the web, discoverability was getting to the top of a search result page. It was then up to the human who visited your page to determine the value of the information, book that table, apply for that passport. As people increasingly rely on AI to find information and complete tasks, discoverability matters in new ways. AI systems need to find the right sources, understand what's useful, and connect people with relevant information – whether that's through an answer, a citation, or a visit to the website itself. Cloudflare's network provides signals that can help OpenAI’s search crawler discover more useful pages across the web to surface to ChatGPT users. OpenAI then independently evaluates and ranks how those pages appear based on how relevant and helpful they are. Together, this creates a feedback loop that can improve both discovery and the quality of information people find. This joint pilot, which used a participating cohort of ~1% of Cloudflare’s total network, has enabled OpenAI to discover and index hundreds of millions of new web pages, helping people discover more useful content and get more questions answered through ChatGPT. By linking back to relevant sources, ChatGPT Search also gives people a way to explore the original content and discover the websites and publishers behind it. With GPT-6 and Intelligent UI, OpenAI is also making ChatGPT an even better place to shop, learn, and find answers, with more visual, interactive experiences tailored to what people need. This work complements these advances by helping ChatGPT discover more useful, up-to-date information from across the web. From discovery to useful answers Finding a URL is only the start. We need to know whether it leads to a page someone can access, whether that page offers anything distinct, and what it might help someone do. We’ve learned, for example, how easily automated traffic can make a nonexistent page look interesting. Bots repeatedly ask for files that aren’t there. Some sites redirect almost any address to their homepage. Other addresses lead to copies of the same content. Recognizing these patterns gives us a way to cut wasted work before a crawler fetches the page, and improve efficiency in a way that benefits site owners. We're also testing signals that identify and flag potentially harmful pages, adding another layer of information to support safer, more reliable discovery. A legitimate site can have a single compromised page, such as a fake login form planted by an attacker. Flagging that one page, rather than the whole domain, keeps people safe without penalizing the site owner. Early results suggest these signals can help identify pages that should be kept out of an index. Making discovery easier As more people use AI to discover information, website owners have new opportunities to reach interested audiences. For those who choose to make their content available to AI systems, these improvements make discovery easier and more efficient. Keeping up by fetching every page more often would be expensive for everyone. For a website owner, a crawler that repeatedly downloads an unchanged page adds load without bringing any benefit. The signals above are how we avoid that. Filtering keeps crawlers away from pages that don't exist or that redirect elsewhere. Change signals tell them when a page is worth another visit, and when it isn't. There's a balance to get right. Finding new pages can initially increase crawling as those pages are evaluated and indexed. The goal is to keep discovering and stay current while reducing the work that takes. For Cloudflare customers, that means less unnecessary load. For OpenAI, it means more of its search resources are spent on information that helps people. Making it worthwhile to participate The next phase will build on what we’ve learned: improve the selection of pages, test faster and more reliable change signals, and measure what happens after content is discovered. We’re continuing to work with OpenAI to understand how better site discovery can translate into real business outcomes, and we’ll keep sharing what we learn along the way. Domain owners’ choices matter throughout. A signal about a page doesn’t grant permission to access it. This research uses metadata about the web for search and discovery, rather than sharing page content for model training. You can use Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control to understand and manage how AI systems access your website.

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.content: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic

items.title: Deploy with Void
items.author: Christoph Nakazawa
items.content:
VoidZero's tools such as Vite, Vitest, Oxc, and Rolldown — bundled in one toolchain as Vite+ — have made frontend development faster, but building full-stack applications requires more than just a tooling stack. These applications need server routes, databases, local development environments, and a fast and easy way to deploy ideas to production. We’re excited to open-source three new products that bring server routing, typed data access, and Cloudflare deployment into a unified Vite workflow. Void Platform: A shared deployment platform for teams to host Void apps on Cloudflare. Void SDK: A composable JavaScript SDK for building full-stack apps with Vite. Void CLI: A CLI for provisioning resources and deploying Vite apps to Cloudflare. The CLI deploys apps built with the SDK to the Platform. All three products are open-sourced as a single JavaScript package and Vite plugin that you can install via npm install void. With Void, you can build your server and client together, carry types from your database to the UI, and let Void automatically provision the Cloudflare resources that your app uses. We originally set out to build a single, private platform for all users to deploy apps to. After VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we adjusted our direction to open-source the platform and allow anyone to install because we saw a growing need: companies want to encourage vibe-coded internal apps, but are concerned about security and do not want to give cloud access to every employee. Void addresses this problem. Void Platform: a cloud platform for your company The Void Platform is fully open source and you can fork it and adapt it to your needs by integrating your company's systems, customize deployment workflows, build features for your customers, or make it work on other deployment platforms. Use the platform as it is, contribute improvements upstream, or fork it and build only the features you need. The open source code can be used out of the box or as a starting point. As an admin of a Void Platform, you control access, set resource limits, inspect deployments and usage through the Void CLI or admin dashboard, and provide guardrails so everyone else can ship serious and vibe coded apps to the same shared platform. By installing a Void Platform, your team or customers have a shared deployment environment in your Cloudflare account on top of Workers for Platforms. Void Platform enables: Faster prototyping. Your team can quickly build prototypes, deploy them, and share working apps for feedback, without setting up a separate Cloudflare account or provisioning resources for every project. This reduces the time to ship internal apps from days/weeks to minutes. Non-technical teams building. This workflow also lets teammates who do not normally write code work with coding agents to build and share their own apps. A designer can create an interactive prototype, or an operations teammate can build an internal dashboard, then deploy it to the same platform. All with the right security measures in place. To self-host a Void platform, you need: A Cloudflare account with Workers for Platforms and R2 enabled A PostgreSQL database An account with your chosen login provider A domain for your apps Then install Void as a cloud platform by running a single command: Once your platform is set up, approved users can connect to it via the Void CLI for deployment. void connect https://api.orange-company.dev A user builds their app using the Void SDK, which is what powers Void Platform benefits like authentication, framework detection, resource provisioning, and more. In other words, Void Platform only works because of the accompanying SDK and CLI. Void SDK: zero-config infrastructure Void turns a Vite app into a full-stack Cloudflare Workers app. You or your agents can write code and Void will automatically infer resource bindings and provision resources such as databases, queues, or AI bindings during deployment. To get started, add Void as a Vite plugin: import { defineConfig } from "vite"; import { voidPlugin } from "void"; import { voidReact } from "@void/react/plugin"; export default defineConfig({ plugins: [voidPlugin(), voidReact()], }); The Void SDK ships with adapters for popular JavaScript UI frameworks such as React and Vue, provides file-based API routing, pre-rendering, caching, islands, and end-to-end type safety from the database to your UI. All of Void’s features are optional and composable. Void integrates with existing application frameworks such as Vinext, React Router, SvelteKit, Nuxt, TanStack Start, and Astro. You can use those frameworks for routing and rendering, while Void handles resource APIs using Hono, migrations, deployment, and authentication with Better Auth. Let's take a look at building a server-rendered page, with types inferred from the database query through to the client: // pages/blog.server.ts import { defineHandler, type InferProps } from 'void'; import { db } from 'void/db'; import { posts } from '@schema'; export const loader = defineHandler(async () => ({ posts: await db.select().from(posts), })); export type Props = InferProps; // pages/blog.tsx export default function Blog({ posts }: Props) { return (
    {posts.map((post) =>
  • {post.title}
    • )}
); } By importing void/db, Void provides a local database to your app during development and makes void deploy provision D1 automatically for you in production. This also works for using AI through Cloudflare’s AI Gateway: just by importing void/ai, everything is set up automatically for you. // routes/api/decide.ts import { defineHandler } from 'void'; import { ai } from 'void/ai'; export const POST = defineHandler(async (c) => { const { question } = await c.req.json(); const result = await ai.run('@cf/cloudflare/clef', { model: 'clef', state: {}, questions: { decision: { type: 'noul', instructions: question }, }, }); const probability = result.answers.decision.noul; return c.json({ answer: probability >= 0.5 ? 'yes' : 'no', probability, }); }); Void's React router is built for Async React, using transitions and Suspense to enable responsive navigation across screens. When you pair this router with a modern data framework such as fate and UI libraries such as Astryx, you can coordinate navigation, data fetching and mutations through React's transitions, as well as actions and optimistic updates across your entire application. Together, these pieces let you build apps that feel synchronous on fast networks, gracefully fall back on slower ones, and keep interactions responsive during expensive rendering updates. If a user does not need Void Platform’s team management features, they can use their own Cloudflare account. Void SDK also deploys to Cloudflare directly. Void CLI: one deployment command The Void CLI is the main interface for Void. The CLI manages the platform and deploys the app. It's built on top of the new cf CLI and works well with agents. With the Void CLI, you can ask your agent to debug failing requests, read deployment logs, analyze how your app is performing, or have them take care of the full lifecycle by deploying a finished app for you. Once your app is ready to deploy to Cloudflare, you can run: The first time you run void deploy, the CLI will prompt you to log into your Cloudflare account. Void builds your app using Vite, applies migrations, automatically provisions resources, and deploys to Cloudflare or a Void Platform. It can be used to handle the full lifecycle of your project such as building, deploying, and managing your resources and projects, for example: Similar to how the CLI, and an agent by extension, can manage the entire lifecycle of a Void app, you can also use the CLI to manage a Void Platform: Manage users, project access, and resources Inspect deployments, logs, and rollbacks Monitor platform health and usage Connect with us VoidZero’s mission is to make JavaScript developers more productive than ever before. We brought Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, Oxfmt, and Vitest together in Vite+ for development, bundling, code quality, and testing. Void extends that stack to full-stack application development, letting you and your agents build, test, and deploy entire applications. We’ve been using the Void SDK, CLI, and Platform in production at VoidZero for the past several months and we are excited to see what you'll build with Void. Please share your feedback with us: Discord: Step into the Void community Discord server for real-time discussions GitHub: Star the repo, start discussions, and report issues Deploy an app with Void: Quick Start Guide X / Bluesky: Follow VoidZero for updates on X or on Bluesky

items.author: Clint Gibler
items.content: Hey there, I hope you’ve been doing well! 🤔 Advice One of the biggest emotional intelligence unlocks I’ve had is learning to differentiate when a partner or friend is wanting to a) vent or b) problem solve. It’s kind of embarrassing, but I think I was late 20’s to early 30’s when that really sunk in. I also noticed that (most) therapists seem to not want to tell you what to do. When I first started therapy, I went in thinking, “OK, you’re an expert in this space and have spent years studying it. I am going to give you my full context and then you can give me an educated, weighted advice and plan based on your knowledge + my specific context.” But it was difficult to get them to give a “this is the answer” or “you should do X” type judgement. After some reflection and further discussion, it makes sense why, though I still kind of find it annoying to be honest. Maybe they’re worried about this: I’ve found long discussions with friends who’ve known me for years really helpful for stuff like this (shout-out my bud Daniel Miessler). I hope you too have friends with whom you’re filling up your relational context window 😂 Sponsor 📣 Personal AI agents are crossing the corporate trust boundary An employee connects their personal AI agent to Slack. Now it can read internal conversations, access files, and act through authenticated sessions. Computer-use agents introduce a new class of unmanaged access that traditional SaaS discovery, EDR and DLP weren't built to address. Harmonic gives security teams visibility into employee AI usage and the sensitive data flowing into AI tools, so you can identify risky behavior without blocking adoption. 👉 Explore Harmonic’s demo portal 👈 Great to get visibility into AI usage while supporting the business, as people will likely work around bans. AppSec Zero to Calc in Six Days: Inside XBOW’s Chrome Full Chain Brendan Dolan-Gavitt describes how XBOW researchers built a Chrome full-chain exploit in six days for $40k in API costs using GPT-5.6 Sol, which received a $250,000 Chrome full-chain reward. The exploit combined a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad, which together turned JavaScript execution in an ordinary Chrome tab into code execution outside the renderer sandbox. 💡 $40K (not including human costs) to make $250K, not too shabby. Hopefully the required token cost to achieve similar exploit capability will rapidly rise for important targets like Chrome, Linux, etc. Grounded or Gamed? We Audited Our Own Cyber Benchmark Semgrep's Brenden Noblitt introduces four metrics (beyond true/false positives and negatives) to evaluate whether LLMs reason about vulnerabilities or just pattern-match. Counterfactual checks whether findings disappear when the vulnerability is patched, metamorphic whether findings persist after renaming identifiers, selectivity whether models avoid flagging safe code with similar structure, and stability whether findings hold across scans. Testing IDOR detection across GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.7, MiniMax M3, Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, and Semgrep Multimodal on a repository with 27 known IDORs, all six models were well-grounded, but every one missed 70% of the real IDORs, and pooling all five LLMs raised union recall to only 29.6%. Models catch textbook IDORs in file-download handlers but miss the same shape on document, prompt, and tool endpoints. 💡 This is cool, I like breaking down and measuring model performance across a number of dimensions, not just TP/FP/FN, etc. I will say 27 IDORs is a bit of a small sample set, and if it’s just one repo, does that mean it’s the same programming language and web framework for each vuln? I also wonder if you add in some repo-specific SECURITY.md or AUTHZ.md context, if the same models would perform significantly better. My intuition says yes but would be neat to test 🤔 Sponsor 📣 CodeAF: open-source software factory with vulnerability hunting built in CodeAF is a new open-source software factory built for open models like DeepSeek and Qwen, with vulnerability hunting built in. Every candidate must survive a challenge before you see it: a source-to-sink trace, a sanitization check, a concrete exploit path. Findings land as SARIF with CWE IDs and a suggested patch. On one open model it tops DeepSource's published OpenSSF CVE Benchmark table on F1. On DeepSWE, same model, it solved nearly 4× as many real GitHub issues as Claude Code, at 3.4× less per solved issue. 👉 Try CodeAF on GitHub 👈 Hm, looks like they’re making some interesting workflow decisions and have a cool design. Looking forward to playing around with it. Cloud Security What Is EntraGoat? A Deliberately Vulnerable Entra ID Simulation Environment Semperis' Jonathan Elkabas and Tomer Nahum released EntraGoat, an open-source deliberately vulnerable Entra ID environment that simulates real-world misconfigurations. The tool uses PowerShell scripts and Microsoft Graph to deploy scenarios including service principal misuse with Graph API permissions, privileged role escalation via application ownership, PIM activation chains and eligible role abuse, dynamic administrative unit poisoning, and certificate authority forgery for Global Admin impersonation. Each challenge starts from an already-compromised identity rather than requiring reconnaissance. AgentCorruption: How A Single Prompt Collapsed The Entire Cloud Security Model Zenity Labs' Tamir Ishay Sharbat and Lana Salameh discovered that AWS Bedrock AgentCore agents could access their instance's IMDS endpoints via SSRF, since the Firecracker microVMs they run in don't isolate network access, allowing an attacker with chat access to extract credentials with a single prompt and compromise all AgentCore agents in the same AWS account and region. The overprivileged default IAM role granted permissions to read all private conversations, pull ECR images, plant persistent memories that hijack agent behavior across future sessions, and extract tool credentials. AWS initially closed the IMDS access report as "informative" after implementing IMDSv2 and left the default role unchanged through two follow-up reviews, only restricting its permissions shortly before publication. Their public statement still calls the behavior documented and expected. Blue Team runZeroInc/sshamble Tool by runZero that finds insecure, unusual, or unique exposures on SSH servers. It inventories authentication capabilities, looks for username-enumeration timing behavior, tests public-key handling, checks the badkeys blocklist, and probes for implementation-specific auth bypasses, pre-auth state transition flaws, or post-session weaknesses. The output is JSONL, which makes it easy to feed into SIEMs or inventory databases for broader asset analysis workflows. Introducing CAIRN: Frontier tracking for AI-integrated malware Cisco Talos' Ryan Fetterman released CAIRN (Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network), a metadata-first hunting toolkit that identifies AI-integrated malware by extracting "cognitive artifacts" like prompt templates, API endpoints, jailbreak strings, and AI provider domains from VirusTotal metadata without downloading binaries. The tool uses 24 acquisition filters to discover samples, a three-tier YARA ontology (T1 for AI artifacts, T2 for behavioral context, T3 for family attribution), semantic clustering with HDBSCAN and UMAP for discovering unknown variants, and relationship graphing to map infrastructure and campaign connections. CAIRN's initial findings reveal an "autonomy escalation arc" from optional LLM features to fully autonomous multi-model orchestrators within a single year, and an AI-analysis evasion technique traced to a red team instructor that reached unrelated actors within 12 months. See also: The Closed Quorum: Inside the first reported autonomous AI C2 implant. Context Collapse, Part 3 - AI Worming through Word Continuing the Context Collapse series, Håkon Måløy shows how a document-borne AI worm works in Microsoft Copilot for Word, where malicious instructions hidden in an external document (as white text on white background) cause Copilot to alter financial figures in generated reports and copy the full attack payload into each downstream document it produces. The hidden text works because Copilot strips all formatting before passing content to the LLM, so text a human can't see is fully readable to the model. Once the payload reaches a second document the original is no longer needed, and the attack spreads through normal workflows across SharePoint, Teams, and OneDrive as each affected document becomes a new carrier. Over 144 days Microsoft deployed two mitigations including a GPT-5.5 model upgrade, but Håkon reproduced the attack class on GPT-5.6 because the problem is architectural, not implementation-specific. 💡 I’ve seen a number of people mention self-propagating AI worms. Hasn’t seen to have been a huge thing yet, but seems feasible 😅 Red Team REA - Reverse Engineer Anything One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior. See a feature you like. Understand how it works, down to the binary level. It leverages a number of existing tools like Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA. 💡 A week or two ago one of my colleagues said, “reverse engineering is basically saturated/solved by current models.” Super cool project. Being able to build so much so quickly, and understand how arbitrary software works is such a cool time for all of us to be in tech. Feeling #blessed. AI for Offensive Security: What Works, What Does Not, and How to Adopt It SpecterOps's Russel Van Tuyl examines how AI is currently being used across their consultants’ offensive security work, covering eight use cases from research and analysis, tool development (LLM-generated Mythic agents and Beacon Object Files), and reconnaissance through BloodHound MCP and DeepPass2 (secret scanner), to social engineering, vulnerability discovery, long-running automation, stealth adaptation, and evidence organization. The team has found roughly 40 previously unknown bugs this way, including LPE, RCE, and a container escape, with work that once took months now taking hours or days. Russel believes web application assessments and external network tests are the best current fits, where results are observable and repeatable enough to validate independently. One common failure mode is that models can satisfy a weak success metric without performing the intended action. Russel's advice is to start with bounded problems and measure workflows where they'll actually run. 💡 Great overview article that also links to other cool research SpectreOps has done 👍️ AI + Security Quicklinks: AI Explained - AI Labs Warn Race Makes Breach ‘Inevitable’ - Great overview of some recent events OAuth risk analysis: Turn 45 minutes into 15 seconds - OAuth grants are multiplying faster than security teams can review them. Until now. Nudge Security AI agents analyze new OAuth grants, return a verdict, show their reasoning, and act only on what you authorize.* Andrej Karpathy - The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening *Sponsored How DigitalOcean Manages Credentials for Autonomous Agents DigitalOcean's Tyler Healy describes their Managed Agents architecture that prevents autonomous agents from ever holding credentials directly, instead brokering access through their Action Gateway at execution time and running agents in isolated microVM sandboxes with zero-egress network policies and non-root execution. For workloads the gateway doesn't broker, three credential tiers decide who can read the value back: env for non-sensitive config, scanned for credential-shaped prefixes like sk- and AKIA. secrets for encrypted storage that still injects the real credential into the sandbox where anything the agent spawns can read it. Scoped secrets that bind a credential to one HTTPS destination so the sandbox only receives a short-lived handle redeemed by an egress proxy. Sub-agents each get their own microVM and resolve their own handle, so a fan-out of fifty sessions carries the same exposure as one, with the whole thing designed to fit NVIDIA's OpenShell policy schema and leave the boundaries in a spec security teams can version. Test-driving Jev on a security task: identity resolution Vincenzo Iozzo evaluates Jev, TypeSafe's “type one thinking” decision model, on identity resolution, the problem of working out which of a company's scattered accounts belong to the same person, comparing it against Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5, a prompted gpt-oss-20b baseline, and traditional entity resolution methods. Jev came out ahead on the large environments at a fraction of the Claude models' cost and roughly ten times their speed, which matters at the scale of a 100,000-account directory. Jev connects JDOE to jane.doe@company.example through the company's naming convention and refuses msmith and msmith1 because the second account exists precisely because a second M. Smith joined. The older methods can't do that, with classic record linkage getting close on tidy directories but falling apart on messy ones, and a supervised classifier trained on four environments collapsing on the fifth. Jev isn't flawless either, since duplicate guest invitations and secondary accounts land in a maybe zone just under its cut-off, though sending those to Sonnet 5 for a second opinion recovers most of them. Misc Prof Gio - You Truly Don't Understand What Just Happened to Mathematics Terence Tao - Math 2.0 - “Particularly in pure mathematics, open problems serve as “lighthouses”: not destinations to be reached in and of themselves, but as useful guides to explore the mathematical landscape around these problems.” “The lessons learned while attempting to solve these problems — whether they succeed, fail, or achieve partial progress — are often more valuable than the final solution to the problem itself.” “Reaching these lighthouses prematurely by automated tools can disrupt the exploration of the paths not taken, and sterilize the surrounding field.” InfoWars HQ ft. Dev Lemons, Graham Platner, Griffin Kelly (Episode 1) - The Onion bought InfoWars, and now they’re creating content 😂 Family of Epstein Victim Appears in Ad Targeting Republican Nikita Bier - Vibe fabricating a dog door with a WiFi-controlled lock, and getting it manufactured SendCutSend - Fast custom parts, at any scale. Sheet metal fabrication, CNC machining, and much more delivered in as little as 24 hours. Get the story. No paywall, no signup. items.title: Rewilding could help vulnerable islands keep pace with rising seas
items.author: Bob Berwyn, Inside Climate News
items.content: Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas. Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham, a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans. Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances, shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments. items.title: How to Design for Failures
items.author: ByteByteGo
items.content: It is impossible to build a failure-proof software system. Sure, a system can go through its lifecycle without any failures. But you can’t provide a guarantee that it will never fail. You might think that if we write perfect code, we can get rid of failures. But writing correct application code is just one part of the problem. Even perfectly written software depends on a physical computer, power availability, working storage, and so on. If the machine loses power, the software will fail no matter how good it is. Therefore, you have to design for failure. This means deciding in advance how a system should behave when some of its parts are not working correctly. In this article, we’ll look at the various strategies that can help developers deal with failures in their systems. Here’s what we will cover: Why adopt an “assume everything breaks” mindset Avoiding faults vs tolerating faults How to figure out the scope of a failure How to reduce the impact of a failure How to handle failures while running the system correctly How to measure recovery from failures Why Assume That Everything Can Break Read more

items.title: Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award
items.content: Ke Mao, Mark Harman, and Yue Jia have been recognized with the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA) 2026 Most Influential Paper Award for their 2016 research, “Sapienz: multi-objective automated testing for Android applications.” The recognition celebrates a decade of impact from work that began at University College London and went on to become testing infrastructure at Meta. Sapienz automatically tests apps to find crashes and helps engineers reproduce them in fewer steps, making failures easier to investigate. The original research combined three goals: exploring more of an app, finding more crashes, and reducing the number of steps needed to trigger them. In its evaluation on 1,000 popular Google Play apps, Sapienz found 558 previously unknown crashes. Within 17 months of publication, Sapienz was deployed at scale at Meta. Today, it runs millions of tests daily across Meta’s platforms, surfaces thousands of unique crashes each week, and helps safeguard hundreds of app releases each month, supporting product reliability and quality. Sapienz’s applications quickly expanded beyond crash detection. By using test accounts with synthetic conversations, it became the app-exploration engine for dynamic taint analysis at WhatsApp. We shared Sapienz’s journey in October in our ISSTA 2026 keynote delivered by Ke Mao, “Finding the Bugs Users Would Find: From Sapienz to Autonomous Agents.” Beyond detecting crashes, large language model (LLM) agents can now explore apps and reason about whether their behavior matches what users should expect, extending automated testing from reliability to functional correctness and, increasingly, automated repair. Sapienz’s core ideas of multi-objective exploration and actionable fault revelation carry over directly. A decade on, those founding principles still hold true. As part of Meta’s overall privacy and risk management program, this work reflects our ongoing efforts to ensure privacy considerations are at the heart of our product development process, helping teams identify risks earlier in the development lifecycle, apply safeguards more consistently, and build privacy protections into each new innovation from the start. The post Sapienz Receives ISSTA 2026 Impact Paper Award appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker
items.author: Crunchbase News
items.content: Methodology This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs. Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs. We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers. If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

items.title: Measuring Human Cryptanalysis Effort
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: Matthew Green has a new site that tries to estimate the number of cryptanalyst-hours that have been spent analyzing different public-key algorithms: Abstract: We estimate how much public cryptanalysis each public-key assumption has received, using the literature itself as the instrument. From roughly sixteen thousand candidate papers we classify cryptanalytic work on ECDLP, structured and plain lattices, syndrome decoding and their comparators, then convert papers into estimated research-allocation years through a person-level author map. These publication-based estimates may substantially overstate actual time spent. Lattices have overtaken elliptic curves in this cumulative measure only recently; we express that history as inference budgets under stated productivity assumptions. The study was conducted by AI models: Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 built the pipeline, ran the analysis and wrote this page, with contributions from GPT-6 Astra. Matthew Green set the questions, made the key methodological decisions and oversaw the work. There are a lot of caveats to this analysis. It relies on published work, so anything unpublished does not count. This includes both academic cryptanalysis that didn’t result in a paper, and intelligence agency cryptanalysis done in secret. But it’s a good first stab at a metric of this sort.

items.title: Rocket Lab announces another delay for its medium-lift Neutron rocket
items.author: Stephen Clark
items.content: Rocket Lab announced Wednesday that its Neutron launch vehicle won't fly until 2027, citing an issue discovered during manufacturing of the rocket's carbon composite structures. The announcement was public confirmation of what nearly everyone inside Rocket Lab and the wider space industry already knew. The most recent official update from Rocket Lab in August suggested the company still held hope of delivering the first Neutron rocket to its launch pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, before the end of this year, a schedule that would have almost certainly pushed the first flight into 2027. But Rocket Lab's statement Wednesday about Neutron's schedule suggests the company is still struggling with manufacturing the rocket's large booster stage. Neutron's reusable first stage is made of carbon composite structures, which offer low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance. But carbon composites in aerospace are generally harder to manufacture than metallic structures. Read full article Comments

items.title: A fully programmable secure web gateway
items.author: AJ Gerstenhaber
items.content: Every secure web gateway on the market works the same way: traffic matches a condition. A terminal action fires. Allow, Block, Isolate, Log. This model has been the foundation of network security for nearly 30 years, and it handles the common case well. But it has a ceiling, and customers with complex environments hit that ceiling regularly. Earlier this year, we shared our vision to build a truly programmable SASE platform. We also outlined how the term programmability has become diluted by the security industry. Most vendors claim programmability because they have public APIs, Terraform providers, webhooks, and alerting. Cloudflare offers all of those things too, but that’s not enough. True programmability means running your own code — arbitrary logic that you wrote for your specific environment — inline in the policy evaluation path, at the moment a security decision is made. Today, we’re excited to announce Cloudflare is bringing true programmability to Cloudflare Gateway and DLP (Data Loss Prevention) by integrating it with the entirety of our edge computing platform. We are releasing a new type of Gateway action, Forward, and custom validation functions, available to all Zero Trust plans. These capabilities allow you to use a Cloudflare Worker to transform and manipulate traffic, or to bring your own data to policy evaluation. The trade-off that every security team faces For as long as firewalls have existed, businesses have faced a binary choice. You can maintain your own security detection engine — your own firewall, your own proxy infrastructure — with high maintenance overhead and low portability, in exchange for maximum customization. Or, you can accept the constraints of a vendor, offloading the considerable maintenance cost, at the expense of flexibility to solve problems specific to your environment. In six years of building Cloudflare Gateway, we have heard from thousands of customers struggling with this trade-off. A security team migrating access controls for a critical internal application needs to inject HTTP headers based on JSON Web Token (JWT) claims from their identity provider. The data exists in the request context, but Gateway cannot read the JWT and write the header. So the team stands up a pool of NGINX proxies solely to perform this transformation. That infrastructure now must be patched, monitored, and secured... indefinitely. Another team wants a Slack notification the moment an employee signs up for a new SaaS service. The policy engine can detect the sign-up event, but it can only Allow or Block. So the team builds a Logpush-to-SIEM-to-Slack pipeline with a 5 to 15 minute delay and no guarantee of delivery. And piles on yet another piece of infrastructure. Dozens of enterprise customers have asked for warning pages that prompt users for justification before allowing access to sensitive destinations. Most then want to customize the ensuing behavior based on additional context about who the user is and the level of access requested. But serving customized, dynamic responses from a policy engine is exceedingly difficult. We have offered customers many extension points over the years. But along with every other firewall vendor, it is impossible to build features to cover threat vectors as quickly as they can appear. However, we also recognize that the best solutions are those which are infinitely extensible to your environment. Why only Cloudflare can solve this problem Cloudflare is not just a firewall, or a secure web gateway, a content delivery network, or an edge service. Cloudflare is a composable compute platform. Cloudflare Workers already allows customers to run complex logic on our network edge from any of our 330+ locations worldwide. Cloudflare Gateway already evaluates and enforces security policy on user traffic at those same locations, on the same machines, in the same data centers. Only Cloudflare runs both distributed customer compute and a full-featured secure web gateway and firewall in the same globally distributed network. We have the unique opportunity and ability to combine those functions into the industry’s first completely programmable and customizable SASE platform. Gateway and Workers were built on the same infrastructure from the beginning. When Gateway forwards traffic to a Worker, that dispatch is a local function call. There is no hairpinning. There is no additional latency from crossing a network boundary. This is the first time that customers will have absolute control over how their proxied traffic is processed, without compromise, using code that they can write and execute without maintaining any sort of infrastructure. Standalone SASE providers without their own compute platform require you to deploy automation in a separate cloud, manually configure webhooks, and accept the round-trip latency and management overhead of stitching together disconnected systems. No other vendor in this space has a programmable edge compute platform co-located with their security gateway. As threats advance at AI-powered speed, this will provide much needed flexibility and agility for security organizations. Two Gateway entry points: Forward action and Custom Functions A new Gateway action type called Forward and a new policy resource called a Custom Function are two distinct ways to call a Worker from a Gateway policy. The Forward action is available in public beta today, and Custom Functions will be available before the end of the year. Forward action: traffic transformation and proxy You can customize HTTP traffic behavior with a new policy action called Forward that routes the matched HTTP request to a Worker as a proxy. Policies with the Forward action are evaluated for traffic allowed by HTTP policies. The first matching Forward rule will then be applied to your traffic, and the traffic will be sent to its bound Cloudflare Worker. The Worker acts as inline middleware: it receives the full headers and request body. Your logic can then choose to modify either one (or take another asynchronous action of some kind), forward the request to the origin, receive the response, can modify that too, and return the final response to the user. import { WorkerEntrypoint } from "cloudflare:workers"; import type { GatewayMiddlewareContext, GatewayMiddlewareNext, } from "@cloudflare/zt-types"; export class GatewayMiddleware extends WorkerEntrypoint { async handle( request: Request, context: GatewayMiddlewareContext, next: GatewayMiddlewareNext, ): Promise<Response> { // Read a value from the Gateway context const clientIP = context.srcIp; // Add headers before the request reaches the origin request.headers.set("X-Gateway-Client-IP", clientIP); // Forward upstream and get the response const response = await next(request); // Modify the response before it reaches the user response.headers.set("X-Processed-By", "gateway-middleware"); return response; } } Gateway handles the TCP connections, TLS termination and re-encryption, certificate management, and HTTP version negotiation. The Worker is responsible only for the transformation logic. You get a customizable, proxy-like extension point for your existing security stack, with none of the operational cost of hosting a traditional HTTP proxy. Your Workers also do not have to transform the request. A rule's sole purpose can be to proxy a request to a Worker that receives the full context of the matched request asynchronously: send a Slack message, write to R2, log to an external pipeline, call a webhook, update a KV store. The traffic can continue to its destination, unbothered. Custom functions: inline policy evaluation A custom function calls out to a Worker inline during Gateway policy evaluation and returns a value. The function is then exposed as a selector in the Gateway policy builder, and the selector is evaluated against its values. The selector is usable in the condition of any network or HTTP Gateway rule, the same way a built-in selector like Source IP or Content Category works today. The Worker receives context about the request: source IP, destination, user identity, device posture, HTTP headers, and more, depending on the policy phase. The Worker returns a typed value (string, number, or boolean) that Gateway uses in rule conditions. The contract is simple: data in, value out. Here is a custom function that parses a JWT Authorization header and returns the user's role: export class GatewayCustomSelector extends WorkerEntrypoint { async compute(ctx: GatewayContext): Promise<string> { const authHeader = ctx.request.headers.get("Authorization"); if (!authHeader) return "anonymous"; const token = authHeader.replace("Bearer ", ""); const payload = JSON.parse(atob(token.split(".")[1])); return payload.groups?.[0] ?? "unknown"; } } With this function deployed, an administrator can create an HTTP policy rule: Custom Function "JWT Role" contains "finance_contractor" with an action of Allow. The custom function becomes part of the rule condition, evaluated alongside every other selector. Custom functions are not limited to HTTP traffic. Because they receive identity, device posture, and connection metadata instead of the full HTTP request, you can use them in the Gateway Network policy rule builder with arbitrary Layer 4 port and protocol traffic as well. The Worker itself can do anything a Worker can already do — call external APIs, read from KV or D1, or invoke Workers AI. But from Gateway's perspective, the function is deterministic: data in, value out. When to use a custom function or a Forward action Custom functions are designed for quick, bounded, stateless evaluations of data which can return a shaped response. You should think of their use similarly to data that can already be evaluated in Gateway selectors; that is, calculations on data that exist within a set of criteria, e.g. “Ports within this range,” or “URL paths that match this regex pattern.” The power comes from being able to extend your structured evaluations with arbitrary or internal sources of data, for which you’ll see some examples below. The Forward action requires a little more planning and preparation. It can be used for powerful transformations inline with users’ live requests, and can manipulate them in complex ways both on the egress and return to the origin service. These should be thought of as transformation functions, something that very few enterprise security proxies even conceptualize today. Workers that use the Forward action should be targeted and designed carefully to avoid adverse effects on the end user’s overall experience. What you can build Purpose justification and interstitial pages A Worker intercepts a request to a sensitive destination and returns an interstitial page requiring the end user to provide a written justification for access. The Worker calls Cloudflare KV to write a session with a TTL, so the user is only prompted once per configured period. It writes the user's identity and their stated justification to Cloudflare D1, creating an audit trail. Or, you can use Hyperdrive to write that record to any internal database you already operate. This has been one of our most-requested features for over four years. With a Worker able to process and manipulate HTTP traffic, it's easy to build to your own standards. Dynamic HTTP header injection A custom function parses a JWT from the request's Authorization header, extracts the user's role or group membership, and returns it as a selector value. A Gateway rule matches on that value and sets an X-App-Role header on the upstream request. No NGINX proxy pool. No additional infrastructure to maintain. File inspection and logging When a file download matches certain criteria, a Worker can send the file to a third-party sandboxing service for detonation and analysis. Or it can write the file in its entirety to Cloudflare R2 as a permanent record for later inspection, without the file ever leaving the Cloudflare network. Real-time alerting on policy match A Worker bound to a Forward policy receives traffic whenever a data loss prevention (DLP) profile matches. The Worker sends a message to a Slack channel or PagerDuty endpoint with the user's email, the rule that fired, and the destination URL. export default { async invoke(ctx: GatewayContext, env: Env): Promise<void> { await fetch(env.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL, { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ text: `DLP alert: ${ctx.identity.email} triggered "${ctx.rule.name}" accessing ${ctx.request.url}` }) }); } } Complex evaluation logic Traditional expression builders for firewalls are not designed for the kind of computation some organizations need at evaluation time. If you maintain internal risk scoring systems that perform behavioral analysis across multiple data sources, or if you have complex maps of users, groups, and conditional memberships where multiple criteria must be independently true, you can use a custom function as the computational extension that evaluates all of that logic and returns a single value to Gateway. Performance and reliability Because Gateway and Workers services run on the same machines in the Cloudflare network, dispatching to a Worker does not introduce a network hop. The performance impact is limited to the execution time of your Worker code itself. When a custom function fails — throws an exception, times out, or returns an unexpected value — you configure the fallback behavior per function. Default values are required in the custom function contract, so that it’s easy to determine behavior. Availability and pricing The Forward action and its integration with Workers are available in a public beta starting today, with Custom Functions expected to be available before the end of the year. At general availability, both will be available for all customers on all plan types. Traffic dispatched to your Workers is billed as standard Worker requests. The feature works with Workers Free, Workers Paid, and Workers for Enterprise with no restrictions on functionality. Workers Free does have execution time limits and daily request limits, which is worth considering as you scale the volume of Gateway traffic you send to your Workers. DLP custom functions for inline detection validation A fully programmable SASE platform extends beyond just Gateway. Our DLP offering — already integrated across Gateway, AI Gateway, Email Security, and more — now supports custom outcomes through integrations with our Compute platform, as well. Most data security products operate by looking for data that matches known patterns. Customers can typically define regular expressions, word lists, or similar to operate these detections. They can also improve confidence in matching through the use of keywords or context analysis on the request body. But these methods have a core flaw: these types of detections can only tell you when something matches the pattern of data relevant to your organization, not whether this specific instance of data is indicative of data exfiltration or misuse. As attackers become increasingly advanced, and agents can be used to ruthlessly exploit systems, improving our ability to accurately detect patterns is not enough. To improve accuracy for the data that matters, you need to know whether the data in question is actively relevant to your organization. To solve this problem, most solutions leverage exact data match, but this comes with its own trade-offs. Customers must prepare, maintain, and transfer reference datasets, then decide how comfortable they are allowing a vendor to manage data from their most sensitive systems. Custom validation functions for DLP bridges that gap, and they’re available starting today. These custom functions allow customers to define their own validation logic, using their own source of truth, directly inside a Cloudflare Worker… and apply it everywhere they use DLP to protect their sensitive data. Credential and secret verification When a DLP detection entry is matched, an outbound Worker can be dispatched to run validation logic prior to a policy enforcement decision. If you have profiles to detect the use of GitHub secrets, but only care about active secrets, you can use a Worker to first look up the status of a detected key, return a response from the appropriate GitHub endpoint, and then decide whether or not the DLP profile should match the traffic. import { DlpValidation, type DlpValidationInput, type DlpValidationResult, } from "@cloudflare/zt-types"; export class DlpValidationEntrypoint extends DlpValidation { async validate({ excerpt, start, end }: DlpValidationInput): Promise<DlpValidationResult> { const bytes = Uint8Array.from(atob(excerpt), (c) => c.charCodeAt(0)); const token = new TextDecoder().decode(bytes.slice(start, end)); const res = await fetch("https://api.GitHub.com/user", { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "User-Agent": "dlp-GitHub-validator", Accept: "application/vnd.GitHub+json", }, }); if (res.ok) return { score: 1.0 }; // token is valid and active if (res.status === 401) return { score: "veto" }; // token is invalid, discard return { score: 0 }; } } What's next This is just the beginning of the fully programmable SASE platform. We are actively working on increasing the entry points from which you can dispatch custom functionality to the entire Cloudflare One suite, with Email Security coming next. That doesn’t mean we’re done building: this new architecture will make it easier for us to build first-party features into all Cloudflare One services faster, more flexibly, and with improved developer experience. It’s also getting easier every day to protect your Workers, agents, and their traffic using Cloudflare One. If you are an Enterprise customer who would like a strategy session for implementation, a preview of the coming functionality, or to be notified about the custom functions beta, please reach out to your account team. Your organizational security can now do anything a Cloudflare Worker can do. We can't wait to see what you build. items.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
items.content: Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. Some highlights: WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second. Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak. Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline. Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6. Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup. Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament. It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern. Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand. Region-Specific Capacity Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament. Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience. During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours. Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality. Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems. Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after. All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics. WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption. That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed. Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t. We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms. We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. We Stay Ready Year-Round Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one. Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second. The post 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
items.content: Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups. To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle. We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t. Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type. That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step. With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it. With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration. When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t. So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change. With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible: Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike. Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers. Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action. The Operating Model That ownership model needs machinery with five key components: Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone. Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke. Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review. Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created. Adapting the Environment to the Models The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from. Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. This gave us three things at once: Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect. Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause. One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions. While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness. Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places: Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself. Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it. Did It Work? Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile: Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults. Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality. Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework. What Worked, and What Did Not Acknowledgements We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions. The post How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
